## Investigate the root cause

When unexpected results occur, do not fix symptoms. Investigate and identify the root cause, prove it with a test, then fix the system under test.

If the coding agent cannot fix the problem after three attempts, stop work and ask the user what to do next.

## Project context

- Read `docs/adr/001-architecture.md` before making architectural changes to elixir-mixir.
- Keep the permanent Elixir/OTP kernel small and prefer standard OTP primitives.
- Distinguish kernel development in the repository from experiments that create and evolve application behavior through MCP.

<!-- Source: rules/20-agent-rules.md -->

## Maintaining agent rules

- Edit project agent instructions in `rules/*.md`; `AGENTS.md` is generated.
- Keep separate topics in separate Markdown files. Files are combined in bytewise filename order; use numeric prefixes to control their order.
- Run `./scripts/build-agent-rules.sh` after adding, changing, or removing a rule file.
- Include the regenerated `AGENTS.md` alongside rule changes.

<!-- Source: rules/30-code-quality.md -->

## Code quality

- Run `mix check` before considering a change complete. It requires formatter compliance, compilation without warnings, strict Credo checks, Doctor documentation coverage, ExUnit tests without warnings, and Dialyzer analysis.
- Format Elixir code with `mix format`; use the committed formatter and Credo configurations.
- Use `ElixirMixir` module namespaces, `CamelCase` module names, and `snake_case` functions, variables, and filenames.
- Keep modules focused, prefer pattern matching and small functions, and use standard Elixir/OTP primitives before adding dependencies.
- Document public modules and functions with `@moduledoc` and `@doc`; add accurate `@spec` annotations to public functions. Internal modules may explicitly use `@moduledoc false`.
- Maintain Doctor's 100% module documentation, function documentation, and typespec coverage baseline, including exception documentation and struct typespecs. Do not exclude modules or lower thresholds to avoid documenting them.
- Write focused ExUnit tests for observable behavior, including failure paths when relevant. Use doctests for executable public API examples and `async: true` only when tests do not share mutable state.
- Fix compiler, Credo, and Dialyzer findings at their cause. Do not blanket-disable checks or suppress warnings to make the quality gate pass.
- Keep development tooling out of production runtime dependencies and commit `mix.lock` when dependencies change.
- Follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` for setup and common development tasks.

<!-- Source: rules/40-commit-messages.md -->

## Commit messages

- Follow the Conventional Commits standard: `<type>[optional scope][!]: <description>`. Use `feat` for features, `fix` for bug fixes, and other appropriate conventional types for other changes. Mark breaking changes with `!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.
- Every commit message must contain a header line, a blank line, and a nonempty commit body.
- Lead with why the software needed to change and why the chosen approach addresses that need. Convey the motivation in the header and explain the reasoning in the body.
- Explain the problem, intent, and relevant tradeoffs instead of repeating what is already apparent from the diff.
- Write for human readers, including future maintainers who do not have the conversation context. Use clear, plain language.

<!-- Source: rules/50-subtask-workflow.md -->

## Complete and commit each subtask

- Work in small subtasks that can each reach a working, independently reviewable state.
- Before continuing to another subtask, finish writing the current subtask's unit tests and ensure they pass. Incomplete or failing tests mean the subtask is not complete.
- Run the full `mix check` quality gate for the current subtask and resolve every failure before continuing. Passing only the focused tests is insufficient.
- Once the unit tests and all quality gates pass, commit the subtask in its working state before starting the next subtask. Keep these checkpoints focused so individual changes can be rolled back easily.
- Follow the commit-message rules and include relevant tests, documentation, and regenerated `AGENTS.md` with the subtask. Leave unrelated user changes out of the commit.
- Use the installed pre-commit hook to enforce the quality gates; do not bypass it to record a failing or unfinished checkpoint.

<!-- Source: rules/60-context-recovery.md -->

## Preserve assignments and recover context

- Before starting an assignment, save its complete instructions under `docs/prompts/` and identify the snapshot in its work plan.
- Before starting a subtask, read the assignment snapshot, governing plan, and subtask document.
- After every context compaction, reread those documents before resuming. A compaction summary does not replace these reads.
- These requirements apply to both planning agents and implementation agents.
- If a planning or task document does not exist yet, read the available governing documents and partial drafts before continuing.
- Preserve assignment snapshots. Record subsequent approved amendments separately and reread them alongside the original snapshot.
- After a complete context clear or in a new session, determine progress from repository state and committed work before continuing.

For Phase 1 planning or implementation, first read `docs/prompts/phase01-planning.md`, then `docs/sdlc/phase01/plan.md` if present, and the current task document. Inspect Git status and relevant commits before resuming. If the current task is unclear, use the plan’s execution order and verify completed prerequisites before selecting the next task.

<!-- Source: rules/70-readme.md -->

## Maintain the public README

- Treat `README.md` as the public entry point for someone who has never used
  elixir-mixir. Explain what the project does, why it is useful, and what a reader
  can try before describing internal components. Define unfamiliar project terms
  and acronyms on first use.
- Write natural, direct prose for a human reader. Use concrete examples and plain
  language. Avoid hype, robotic phrasing, unexplained jargon and internal task or
  checkpoint language. Make only claims supported by current behavior and evidence.
- When a change affects public capabilities, setup, commands, example prompts,
  requirements or limitations, update the README in the same verified commit.
  Check whether an update is needed; unrelated internal changes do not require
  README churn. Keep current features distinct from future plans.
- Keep a short, usable path from setup to a first successful experiment. Startup
  instructions must include a readiness wait before connecting the client. Explain
  where commands run, required tools and platform assumptions. Keep example prompts
  concrete, consistent with supported MCP behavior, and clear about expected results
  and existing-worker conflicts when they form a sequence.
- Preserve clear explanations of in-memory state, client versus runtime lifetime,
  and generated-code isolation limits. Link to detailed API, architecture,
  contribution and demonstration documents instead of copying their internals into
  the introduction. Verify local links and affected examples when editing.
